topics.title: Section 498A
bullets: On 3 August 2026, the SC held that Section 498A (now Section 85 BNS) applies to live-in relationships that are "in the nature of marriage" with an "intent to marry".
A bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and N Kotiswar Singh held that denying criminal protection to women in such relationships is offensive to Article 14.
The Court observed: "Cruelty... does not check at the door, whether the house it enters is that of a married woman or not". Background –
Section 498A was introduced into the Indian Penal Code in 1983 to address domestic cruelty against married women.
The provision penalises a husband or his relatives for subjecting a woman to cruelty, including physical and mental harassment.
It was enacted to tackle the growing menace of dowry harassment and domestic violence, which were not adequately covered by existing laws.
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 was enacted to provide civil remedies for women facing domestic violence.
It recognises "relationships in the nature of marriage" , covering live-in relationships and providing protection to unmarried women.
The Act offers remedies like maintenance, protection orders, and residence rights, but is a civil legislation without criminal sanctions.
In 2014, the Supreme Court in Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar laid down guidelines to prevent arbitrary arrests under Section 498A.
The Court held that no arrest should be made without preliminary inquiry by the Investigating Officer.
These safeguards were introduced to curb the misuse of Section 498A as a tool for harassment and settling personal scores.
In 2023, Parliament enacted the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) to replace the Indian Penal Code.
Section 498A of the IPC was replaced by Sections 85 and 86 of the BNS .
The new provisions retained the substance of Section 498A while modernising the criminal justice framework.
Because Section 498A explicitly uses the word "husband" , its application was traditionally restricted to legally valid marriages .
Over the years, the Supreme Court expanded this definition to cover men who induced a woman into a void or voidable marriage (e.g., by hiding a previous marriage) .
Courts have held that live-in relationships are not illegal; they are protected under Article 21 as part of an adult's right to life and personal liberty .

However, India has no dedicated law for live-in couples. Protections exist through judicial precedents, such as the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, which covers "relationships in the nature of marriage" .
Courts also recognise children born from such relationships as legitimate and entitled to inheritance, and a woman can claim maintenance from her partner .
Uttarakhand: The state Assembly passed the UCC Act in February 2024, and the rules were implemented in January 2025 .
Gujarat: The state Assembly passed the UCC Bill in March 2026 .
Assam: The UCC Bill was tabled in the state Assembly in May 2026 .

Registration: All three states make registration mandatory. Uttarakhand and Assam require registration within one month; Gujarat also requires registration, with similar penalties for non- compliance .
Rights of Partners and Children: All states recognise children born from live-in relationships as legitimate, and allow deserted partners to claim maintenance through courts . Case –
Lokesh B.H. v. State of Karnataka, arose from a complaint by a woman who alleged that Dr. Lokesh B.H. had married her in 2010 after concealing his prior marriage .
She accused him and his relatives of dowry harassment, cruelty, and attempting to set her on fire .
Lokesh argued that since his alleged second marriage was void (as his first marriage was still subsisting), he could not be treated as her "husband" under Section 498A .
The Karnataka High Court rejected Lokesh's argument and refused to quash the criminal proceedings .
The High Court held that when a man induces a woman to believe she is lawfully married to him, and then subjects her to cruelty, he cannot evade criminal responsibility .
This led Lokesh to appeal to the Supreme Court . SC Judgment –
The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and held that Section 498A applies to live-in relationships in the "nature of marriage" .
It gave a purposive interpretation to the word "husband," keeping in view the reformative and socially beneficial intent of the Section .
The Court held that a woman's marital status has no proximate link to the objective of preventing cruelty in a household setting .
The Court reasoned that if a woman faces cruelty from her partner, it makes no logical sense to offer her protection if she is married, but deny it if she is cohabiting before marriage .
This distinction, the Court held, "has no rational nexus with the object of preventing domestic violence and is as such offensive to Article 14 of the Constitution of India" (Right to Equality) .
The Court clarified that not every live-in relationship would attract criminal liability .
The couple must, in addition to being in a "relationship in the nature of marriage" , also have the "intent to marry“.
The Court borrowed the concept of a "relationship in the nature of marriage" from the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 .
The Court held that the initial burden of proof to establish the "intent to marry" will lie on the female partner seeking protection .
The Court did not lay down specific parameters for how this internal "intent" is to be legally recognised .
This means courts will determine the existence of "intent to marry" on a case-by-case basis .
Both the petitioner and the Union Government argued that unmarried women are already protected under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 .
The Supreme Court rejected this argument, pointing out the fundamental difference between the two laws .
The DV Act is primarily a civil legislation providing remedies like maintenance and protection orders, whereas Section 498A creates criminal liability for acts of cruelty .
The Court directed that the safeguards laid down in the Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) judgment shall be strictly applied .
No live-in partner or relative accused of cruelty in such a relationship shall be arrested without preliminary inquiries .
This ensures that the law is not misused as a means of settling scores or ventilating grievances .
The Court clarified that its ruling is confined to Section 498A and should not be automatically extended to other penal provisions .
The proposition of law as laid down shall be limited to Section 498A IPC only .
Different statutory language or legislative intent may apply to other provisions .
The Court held that not only the live-in partner, but his relatives too can be prosecuted under Section 498A .
The Court said: "no person... being either the live-in partner 'in the nature of marriage' or his relative, shall be arrested without preliminary inquiries" .
This ensures that women in live-in relationships have the same protection against in-laws as married women .

topics.title: Semiconductor Mission 2.0
bullets: On 15 July 2026, the Union Cabinet approved ISM 2.0 with an outlay of ₹1.27 lakh crore (~$13.23 billion), significantly expanding the first phase.
The mission aims to position India as a reliable player in the global semiconductor value chain, advancing Aatmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India.
ISM 2.0 focuses on indigenous chip design, fabrication, and supply chain resilience, building on 12 projects with ~₹1.64 lakh crore investment. Background –
The Union Cabinet approved the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) 1.0 in December 2021 with an outlay of ₹76,000 crore to build a sustainable semiconductor and display ecosystem.
A specialized and independent India Semiconductor Mission was set up as the nodal agency for the efficient implementation of semiconductor and display schemes.
The programme offered up to 50% fiscal support to attract investments in chip fabrication, packaging, and design.
In June 2023, the government approved Micron Technology's $2.75 billion ATMP facility in Sanand, Gujarat - the first project under ISM 1.0.
Later in 2023, India approved its first silicon fabrication unit - a Tata Group-PSMC joint venture in Dholera, Gujarat, with an investment of nearly $11 billion (~₹91,000 crore).
By 2025, 12 semiconductor projects with cumulative investments of ~₹1.64 lakh crore had been approved across six states.
The Tata Electronics-PSMC fab in Dholera, Gujarat, is India's first commercial-grade chip facility, expected to have a monthly capacity of 50,000 wafers across 28nm to 110nm technologies .
Tata Electronics is also building a semiconductor assembly and testing facility in Jagiroad, Assam, with an investment of over ₹27,000 crore, capable of manufacturing 48 million chips per day .
The Micron Technology assembly plant in Sanand, Gujarat, started commercial production in February 2026 .
Kaynes Semicon in Sanand, Gujarat, a ₹3,300 crore OSAT facility inaugurated in March 2026, has a capacity of 60 lakh chips per day for EVs and industrial applications.
The HCL-Foxconn joint venture is setting up a ₹3,700 crore OSAT facility in Jewar, Uttar Pradesh, with operations expected by 2028, producing display driver chips.
Other key facilities include CG Semi (₹7,600 crore), SiCSem (₹2,066 crore), 3D Glass Solutions (advanced 3D packaging), and Crystal Matrix (first display assembly facility).
India's semiconductor market has grown from $38 billion in 2023 to $45–50 billion in 2024-25 and is projected to reach $100– 110 billion by 2030 .
By 2025, the market is estimated at $54.3 billion and expected to touch $103.5 billion by 2030 at a 13.8% CAGR .
India is targeting 70–75% self-sufficiency in domestic chip demand by 2029 and aims to become a leading semiconductor nation with 3 nm and 2 nm manufacturing capabilities by 2035.
Currently, 105 startups are already developing semiconductor chips, with the focus now shifting to creating indigenous intellectual property (IP), chip designs, and complete semiconductor systems .
315 universities are training students using industry-standard Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools, with nearly 68,000 students trained so far.
India already has over 250,000 semiconductor professionals, with 58,000+ new job postings in 2024-25 . Recent News –
On 15 July 2026, the Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the second iteration of India Semiconductor Mission (ISM 2.0) .
The total outlay for ISM 2.0 is ₹1.27 lakh crore - a sharp increase from the ₹76,000 crore allocated under ISM 1.0 .
The mission's term has been extended from five to twelve years, aimed at giving long-term policy certainty to global and domestic investors .
The government will attract investments of around ₹4 lakh crore.
It aims to achieve semiconductor production worth ₹2 lakh crore during the scheme period .
Incentives have been restructured: 40% for silicon fabs, 35% for other fabs, 35% for advanced packaging, and 25% for conventional packaging .
As India's first silicon fab is scheduled to be commissioned in 2028, the government plans to attract additional investments in semiconductor fabrication units .
Support under ISM 2.0 will extend to various manufacturing facilities, including silicon fabs, compound semiconductor fabs, discrete component fabs, and display fabs.
By 2035, India aims to be among the top semiconductor nations globally.

Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw outlined three priorities: ➢supporting design companies and startups, ➢building the full ecosystem from equipment to materials and testing, and ➢deepening the talent base
The Digital India RISC-V Programme promotes open-source processor development without licence costs, reducing dependence on proprietary architectures.
The programme aligns with India's goals of technological sovereignty and self-reliance in critical digital infrastructure.
This initiative is part of India's broader push to develop indigenous microprocessor capabilities.
The Chips to Startup Programme enables access to advanced design tools and fabrication for universities and startups.
This initiative aims to democratise chip design and encourage innovation at the grassroots level.
105 startups and MSMEs have been provided access to industry- standard EDA tools through this programme .
ISM 2.0 will support economic growth across all sectors and strengthen national security through enhanced supply chain resilience .
India is developing indigenous microprocessors such as DHRUV64 to reduce dependence on imported chips.
Domestic chip production reduces India's vulnerability to foreign supply disruptions and strengthens its strategic autonomy.
The global semiconductor market is projected to exceed $1–1.5 trillion by 2030, driven by a massive AI-driven supercycle .
Currently, China, South Korea, and Taiwan dominate the production chain, operating specialised, capital-intensive foundries.
India's emergence as a semiconductor hub offers a geopolitically stable alternative to existing manufacturing hubs, aligning with global supply chain diversification trends.
